title.en: Soulsville U.S.A.: Stax and southern soul
title.zh: 美国灵魂乐镇Stax和南方灵魂乐

summary.en: Memphis’s Stax label shapes southern soul and, with Atlantic, carries it into wider circulation.
summary.zh: 位于孟菲斯的Stax厂牌开创了南方灵魂乐，并与Atlantic厂牌合作使其发扬光大。

body.zh:
位于孟菲斯的Stax厂牌开创了南方灵魂乐，并与Atlantic厂牌合作使其发扬光大。

我们已经讨论了Motown在1960年代中期的黑人流行乐中所扮演的角色，现在让我们将注意力转到美国灵魂乐镇（Soulville, USA）Stax和南方灵魂乐 (southern soul) 上。为了展开讨论，我们先来看看Atlantic Records发生了什么。Altantic Records是我们讨论的摇滚史中最重要的厂牌之一，当然，他们创立得很早，甚至能追溯到摇滚诞生之前。他们起初以发行R&B音乐为主，之后在第一次摇滚浪潮中起了相当重要的作用，即1960年到1964年那段时间。他们旗下有很多像Ben E King、The Drifters这样的大人物。因此Atlantic Records非常重要。
接下来我们谈谈在60年代期间发生了什么。当然从60年代末到70年代早期，他们成了签约众多摇滚大牌的厂牌之一，例如Led Zeppelin以及许多类似的乐队都和Atlantic Records签约了。但是彼时60年代，Atlantic Records正在开始从甜灵乐（sweet soul）转型至主打南方灵魂乐。sweet soul大家应该记得这个风格，代表人物有Ben E King、The Drifters等等。这是一种非常优雅含蓄的音乐风格，它将R&B与弦乐融合，有时还加入拉丁节拍等。然而南方灵魂乐则是一种更加热情的音乐类型，无拘无束，受福音音乐（Gospel）的影响很大，它看起来更为自然且不加修饰，尽管唱片中通常都修缮了大部分粗粝的部分。当Wexler包装一位名叫Solomon Burke的艺人时，就开始朝这个方向发展。Burke也和Bert Berns共事，当谈到Atlantic在1963年发行了登上R&B单曲榜第二名的《If You Need Me》时，我们多次谈到了Bert Berns，这首歌就是Solomon Burke演唱的。Solomon还在1965年以《Got To Get You Off My Mind》拿到了R&B单曲榜冠军。但是Jerry Wexler作为Atlantic当时的负责人之一，开始发现除了为Altantic旗下的艺人制作之外，如果能发掘出一些地区性的流行单曲然后取得授权，也能获得巨大成功。我们已经谈过国家范围内授权热单的概念，所以Atlantic可以将一首歌重新包装，从一个小点的厂牌手中买到版权，把一个地区性的流行歌曲变身为全国性的强势热单。因此Wexler开始寻找那些可以让Atlantic Records以其他可能的形式重新发行并且成为热曲的歌，他开始和孟菲斯的Stax Records合作。
Stax在1960年由Jim Stewart和他姐姐Estelle Axton创立，你可以看到取Stewart的“ST”和Axton的“AX” 合在一起，就成了Stax。在田纳西州的孟菲斯，他们开始售权由Atlantic Records来进行分销。那时他们和 Jerry Wexler生意上关系密切，同时也和Atlantic Records的传奇录音师Tom Dowd关系密切。Tom被下派到Stax在孟菲斯的录音棚，负责改善和维修他们的录音设备，Dowd对Atlantic的唱片质量非常上心，尽管他们现在将更频繁地使用Stax的录音棚了，Dowd希望确定设备能够达到自己所要求的标准。
所以当我们谈到Stax， 我们通常会从Stax厂牌和Stax录音棚说起。但是稍后你将发现，这种情况更加广泛，包括了南方的其他地方甚至纽约在内的其他录音室，都是普遍的南方灵魂乐风格。不论这些唱片是否真的在南方录制，还是说只是一种名义上的叫法，人们常用Stax来指代它。有时候大家也常用Volt这个厂牌来代表它，Volt是Stax旗下的子厂牌。Stax和Volt代表了一种风格，更确切地说它指的是这些厂牌旗下的艺人。
让我感兴趣的不仅仅是南方灵魂乐，同时还有Motown和Stax之间的关系。因为很多时候Motown和Stax两家厂牌建立的方式就像两个极端，我们在序言中谈到了这一点。Motown的特点是为了白人听众背叛黑人文化，而Stax的音乐则往往被认为更真实，因为它更靠近于黑人传统和福音音乐，更是一种无拘无束的类型。但是令人吃惊的是，尽管两家厂牌之间有许多非常明显的差异，但是他们的行事方式是多么相近。首先是Stax有许多全身心投入的歌曲创作人和制作人，尽管不是以Berry Gordy的那种非常有组织的形式存在。Issac Hayes和David Porter两人一起，既是歌曲创作者又是Sam & Dave的制作人。还有Steve Cropper（录音室乐队的吉他手）与Otis Redding合作密切，所以就是一些人写歌，一些人表演的景象。其中最大的相似之处，就在于这些录音室乐队。关于Motown我们提到过Funk Brothers，但是关于位于孟菲斯的Stax录音室，我们就要提到Booker T. & the M.G.'s。他们四个人算得上是黑人流行乐历史中的传奇人物。Booker T. Jones弹风琴，Steve Cropper弹吉他，Duck Dunn弹贝斯，AI Jackson Jr. 打鼓。Booker T. & the M.G.'s有他们自己的器乐热单，《Green Onions》可能是最出名的一首。他们也是许多Stax旗下组合的幕后合作乐队， 这甚至是一个比我们在Motown看到的更为宽松融洽的情况。很多时候在Stax，他们不仅和艺人们合作，同时他们也进行创作，渐而创造了一种非常融洽的环境。要记得，在类似Atlantic厂牌的这些地方，规矩是把人找来给他们看排行榜，然后这些音乐人会为了榜单写打榜歌曲，就像回到了四五十年代的big band时期。
另外当我们谈到Stax，就必须说到号（horn）的使用，号并没有出现在所有Stax发行的唱片中，但却足以使其流行起来。从20世纪60年代，人们开始谈论号角乐队，这相当具有影响力。当The Beatles制作《Got to Get You Into My life》这首歌时，Paul McCartney曾考虑使用号带来密集的节奏。这也是Stax标志性的一部分，人们常常用“Stax horn”来指代这种声音。接下来让我们把注意力转到Stax旗下的一些艺人。
body.en:
Memphis’s Stax label shapes southern soul and, with Atlantic, carries it into wider circulation.

We have covered Motown’s role in mid-1960s Black pop; now turn to Soulsville, U.S.A.—Stax—and southern soul. To open, what happens at Atlantic Records. Atlantic is one of the most important labels in our rock history; it starts early, even before rock. It begins in R&B, then plays a major role in the first rock wave—especially 1960–1964. Acts like Ben E. King and the Drifters matter. So Atlantic matters.
What happens in the 1960s: by the late 1960s–early 1970s Atlantic becomes a home for major rock acts—Led Zeppelin and others. But in the 1960s Atlantic is shifting from sweet soul toward southern soul. Recall sweet soul: Ben E. King, the Drifters—elegant, restrained R&B with strings, sometimes Latin rhythms. Southern soul is hotter, freer, heavily gospel-influenced, sounding more natural and unadorned—though records usually polish away much of the roughness. When Jerry Wexler packages Solomon Burke, the turn begins. Burke also works with Bert Berns—we have mentioned Berns often; Atlantic’s 1963 “If You Need Me,” No. 2 R&B, is Burke. Solomon also takes 1965’s “Got to Get You Off My Mind” to No. 1 R&B. Wexler, then a key Atlantic head, sees that besides cutting Atlantic artists, licensing regional hits can also succeed. We have covered national licensing of hits: Atlantic can re-package a song bought from a smaller label and turn a regional smash into a national one. So Wexler looks for records Atlantic can reissue in other forms as hits—and begins working with Memphis’s Stax.
Stax is founded in 1960 by Jim Stewart and his sister Estelle Axton—ST from Stewart, AX from Axton. In Memphis, Tennessee, they sell distribution rights to Atlantic. They work closely with Jerry Wexler and with Atlantic’s legendary engineer Tom Dowd. Dowd is sent to Stax’s Memphis studio to improve and maintain the gear; he cares about Atlantic’s sound quality, and though they will use Stax’s rooms more often, he wants equipment up to his standard.
When we say Stax we usually mean label and studio. But you will see the story is wider: other southern rooms and even New York work in a general southern-soul style. Whether records are truly cut in the South or only in name, people often use Stax as the shorthand—sometimes Volt, Stax’s subsidiary. Stax and Volt name a style, or more precisely the artists under those labels.
What interests me is not only southern soul but Motown–Stax relations. The two labels are often cast as extremes—as in the preface. Motown is said to betray Black culture for white listeners; Stax is said to sound more authentic, closer to Black tradition and gospel, freer. Yet despite clear differences, their working methods are strikingly similar. Stax has committed writers and producers, if not in Gordy’s highly organized form. Isaac Hayes and David Porter write and produce Sam & Dave. Guitarist Steve Cropper works closely with Otis Redding. Some write, some perform. The biggest parallel is the house band. Motown has the Funk Brothers; Stax’s Memphis studio has Booker T. & the M.G.’s—four legends in Black pop history. Booker T. Jones on organ, Steve Cropper guitar, Duck Dunn bass, Al Jackson Jr. drums. They have their own instrumental hits—“Green Onions” the best known—and back many Stax acts, in an even looser, more collaborative atmosphere than Motown. At Stax they often write as well as play, building a tight creative room. Remember: at places like Atlantic the old rule is bring people in, show them the charts, write for the charts—like big-band days of the 1940s–50s.
Talking Stax also means horns. Horns are not on every Stax release, but enough to define the sound. From the 1960s people talk horn sections with real influence. When the Beatles make “Got to Get You into My Life,” Paul McCartney thinks about dense horn rhythm. That is part of the Stax stamp; people often say “Stax horns.” Next: some Stax artists.
